reason: Spores are small or large. The 'lumina small' and 'minute spheres' examples describe sculpture, not the spore, so a rule is needed to ignore them.
A pale or pallid plant is a normal colour statement for the whole plant.
A staminode can be square or four-angled. 'Subsquare' is a fair reading.
Endocarps can be spiny. The examples mention spines, prickles and echinulate surfaces.
A pedicel can be wide or widened toward the apex.
Wrong bearer. FLOPO_0985028 is a pinnule. The examples describe the margin teeth and the apex of the pinnule, not the pinnule as a whole. These should go to the margin or tooth, or to a rule.

'Concolorous' means the same colour as another part (the lamina or the other side). The pair is only right when that comparison is kept. A rule would need to tell concolorous from discolorous and say what it is compared with.
An achene can be narrow. Some examples ('base narrow', 'body narrow') describe a sub-part, but the pair itself is fine.
Wrong reading. 'Prophyllate' says the axis or flower bears a prophyll. It does not say the prophyll itself is present. The bearer is the axis, flower or inflorescence.
A spike can be subglobose or spheroid.
Raceme axes and branches can be pilose, villous or glabrescent.
Peristome teeth are often recurved, and moss floras say so.
A capsule can be pendent or horizontal. That is a standard moss and fruit statement.

A measured value ('1.5 mm thick') belongs under the attribute thickness (PATO_0000915). It does not belong under increased thickness. This is a wrong reading, and a rule for measurements would fix it.
Hyaline cells in Sphagnum are described as rhombic or rhomboidal.
An embryo can sit at the apex or terminal end of the seed or albumen. 'Embryon apical' says that.
Legumes can be asymmetric, for example at the base.
A moss operculum (lid) can be orbicular or suborbicular.
Staminate flowers can be small.
Lodicules can be subulate.
Secondary veins can be concave (sunken) on the upper face.
An androphore (stalk of the stamens) can be pubescent. The examples describe it correctly.
A floral disc can have a measured thickness, and thickness is the right attribute for a measurement.
Trichomes can be dimorphic or monomorphic. This is a morphology statement about the trichomes. There is only one flora, so confidence is low.
Bracteoles can be filamentous.
Perianth or corolla lobes can be incurved, and curved covers that.
PATO_0000001 is the root 'quality' term and says nothing. The examples are about posture (erect, drooping) or branching, which need their own terms.
Wrong part. A perianth is not sessile. 'Perianth sessile' means the flower has no stalk, so the bearer is the flower or the pedicel.
Leaf teeth can be straight or curved.
A midvein can be pale or paler than the blade.
'Lax' blades (limp) are different from 'loose' teeth. The examples mix the two. A rule would need to separate lax or flaccid texture from loose arrangement of sub-parts.
A spike can be compact or dense. 'Compressed' is a different meaning (flattened), so a rule should keep 'compact' and drop 'compressed'.
A pappus (or its bristle bases) has a measurable width.
A pappus can be hyaline, meaning translucent.
Wrong part. The examples say the midnerves are evident, so the bearer is the nerve, not the bract.
Involucral bracts can be dilated or expanded at the apex.
Bracts can be rudimentary or vestigial.
Leaf teeth can be acuminate.
Orchid gynostemia can be spotted, but the examples ('ventral surface', 'at base') may describe the lip or petals. A rule would need the bearer to be the column itself.
A seed can be square. The 'strophiole squarish' example is another part, so a rule should drop it.
The adaxial epidermis of a petiole can be hairy (villous, hirsute, puberulent).
A hypanthium can be bristly.
Seed cones have a shape, and that is the attribute term.
Tubercles can be elongate.
An inflorescence axis (such as a rachilla) can be winged.
A capsule apex can be emarginate. One example, 'not indented', is a negation, so a rule should handle it.
An operculum or its beak can be blunt.
Fruit valves can be pubescent.
Perianth bristles can be equal or unequal in size.
Wrong part. The examples say the angles or ribs are prominent. The bearer is the angle or rib, not the achene.
Stolons can be short.
Bracts can enclose or surround flowers or an inflorescence.
Cyathia can be solitary or clustered. That is an arrangement statement.
Wrong part. The shape ('involucre obconic') belongs to the involucre as a whole, not to a single bract.
A seed coat can be mucilaginous (mucoid).
Epicalyx bracts have a length.
A corolla (throat or tube) can be flared.
A hypanthium can be bilaterally symmetric.
A staminal tube or column can be exserted.
A leaf apex can be recurved.
